items.title: Section: Four Modes of Skilful Cultivation — How Resolute, Thorough, and Constant Practice of the Perfections Shapes the Body

items.zh: 復次，略說在家、出家二分菩薩，所有四種善修事業，當知能感一切相好。謂於此中決定修作，能感足下善安住相。委悉修作，能感足下千輻輪相、立手摩膝、手足網縵、身皮細滑、於其身上七處皆滿、肩善圓滿、膊間充實、身分洪直、其舌廣薄。恒常修作，感纖長指、足跟趺長、身不僂曲、其身圓滿如諾瞿陀、其齒無隙。
items.en:
Second, briefly explaining skilful cultivation; first, distinguishing the marks individually; first, stating [the point]. Furthermore, briefly stated, the four kinds of skilful cultivation possessed by bodhisattvas — whether lay or renunciate — should be known to bring about all the marks and exemplary signs together.
Commentary: the four kinds of skilful cultivation are: bodhisattvas practising the six perfections with resolute cultivation, thorough cultivation, constant cultivation, and faultless cultivation — these are called the four kinds of skilful cultivation.
Second, explaining; first, resolute cultivation. Resolute cultivation here brings about the mark of feet resting well upon the ground.
Second, thorough cultivation. Thorough cultivation brings about the wheel-marked soles, hands reaching past the knees, webbed hands and feet, fine smooth skin, fullness in the seven places on the body, well-rounded shoulders, full flesh between the shoulders, an upright proportioned body, and the broad, thin tongue.
Third, constant cultivation. Constant cultivation brings about slender long fingers, the full raised instep, a body that never stoops, a body proportioned like a banyan tree, and teeth without any gap.

items.title: Section: Faultless Cultivation — Eighteen Marks Arising from a Mind Free of Any Attachment to Fame or Recognition

items.zh: 無罪修作，能感餘相。當知此中，於諸有情無損加行，由此能感手足細軟、身皮細滑。於諸善中次第加行、應時加行，由此感得瑿泥耶𨄔。深生歡喜，極光淨心現行諸善，由此感得常光一尋、身皮金色、其齒鮮白、眉間白毫。不依稱譽聲頌修善，覆藏己德，由此能感勢峯藏密。所修善根迴向菩提，由此感得身毛上靡、具四十齒皆悉齊平、於諸味中得最上味、其頂上現烏瑟膩沙。修善無厭無劣加行，由此感得其身上分如師子王、頷如師子。於諸有情，以利益心平等瞻視，得齒齊平、目紺青色、睫如牛王。於下劣善不生喜足，起勝加行，由此因緣，得大梵音，言詞哀雅能悅眾意，譬若羯羅頻迦之音，其聲雷震猶如天鼓。如是四種善修事業，能得菩薩三十二種大丈夫相殊勝清淨。
items.en:
Fourth, faultless cultivation; first, stating [the point]. Faultless cultivation brings about the remaining marks.
Second, explaining, in eight parts; first, causing no harm to any being. Know that causing no harm to any being brings about soft, supple hands and feet, and fine, smooth skin.
Second, cultivating goodness in sequence and at the fitting time. Cultivating goodness in sequence among wholesome things, at the fitting time, brings about calves like a deer-king's own.
Third, a deeply joyful, radiant, pure mind manifesting goodness. A deeply joyful mind, radiant and pure, manifesting goodness, brings about the constant one-fathom radiance, golden skin, brilliantly white teeth, and the white ūrṇā between the brows.
Fourth, cultivating goodness without reliance, concealing one's own virtue. Not relying on praise or renown in cultivating goodness, concealing one's own virtue, brings about the concealed mark.
Fifth, dedicating one's cultivated wholesome roots to awakening. Dedicating one's cultivated wholesome roots to awakening brings about hair curling upwards, forty perfectly even teeth, obtaining the finest of every flavour, and the crown protrusion appearing atop the head.
Sixth, cultivating goodness without satiation or inferior effort. Cultivating goodness without satiation and without inferior effort brings about the upper body like a lion-king's own, and cheeks full as a lion's own.
Seventh, benefiting all beings with equal regard. Regarding all beings with a mind of benefit and equal regard obtains even teeth, eyes of deep blue-black, and lashes like a bull-king's own.
Eighth, not feeling satisfied with inferior goodness. Not feeling satisfied with inferior goodness, arousing a more excellent effort, by this cause and condition obtains the great, resonant voice, its words moving and elegant, delighting all who hear, like the kalaviṅka bird, thunderous as a heavenly drum.
Third, concluding. These four kinds of skilful cultivation together bring the bodhisattva's thirty-two marks of a great being to excellent, complete purity.

items.zh: 當知如是三十二種大丈夫相、八十隨好，菩薩若在種性地中，唯有種子依身而住。菩薩若在勝解行地，始能修彼能得方便。菩薩若在清淨增

items.title: Section: Purity Deepens Ground by Ground to Buddhahood, and Why Only the Thirty-Two Marks Bear the Name "Great Being"

items.zh: 上意樂地中，乃名為得。菩薩若在諸餘上地，如是相好轉勝清淨。若在如來到究竟地，當知相好善淨無上。如是諸相是有色故，劣中勝品諸有情類易了知故，雖有一切不共佛法皆得名為大丈夫相，唯立此為大丈夫相。又即如是三十二種大丈夫相，由所依性能任持故，由極殊妙令端嚴故，說名隨好。
items.en:
Fourth, all remaining higher grounds. At every remaining higher ground, the marks and exemplary signs grow progressively more excellent and pure.
Fifth, the ground of the Tathāgata. Upon reaching the ultimate ground of the Tathāgata, know that the marks and exemplary signs are utterly excellent, pure, and unsurpassed.
Second, clarifying establishment and non-establishment. These marks possess visible form, easily recognised by beings of lesser, middling, and superior kind; although all the exclusive buddha-qualities could be called marks of a great being, only these are established under that name.
Third, explaining how the name arose. Also, these thirty-two marks of a great being, because the basis they depend upon sustains and upholds them, and because their extreme subtlety and wonder makes them dignified, are called "exemplary signs."

items.title: Section: The Staggering Scale of Merit — From a Single Pore to the Great Dharma-Conch Mark of the Voice

items.zh: 又於此中以要言之，一切有情福聚量等爾所福聚，能感如來一毛孔處。乃至一切所有毛孔隨入福聚爾所福聚，能感如來一種隨好。乃至一切所有隨好隨入福聚，增至百倍爾所福聚，能感如來相中一相。乃至一切所有諸相隨入福聚，除白毫相、烏瑟膩沙，增至千倍爾所福聚，能感如來眉間白毫。乃至白毫隨入福聚，增至百千倍爾所福聚，能感如來其頂上現烏瑟膩沙無見頂相。乃至白毫隨入福聚，增至俱胝百千倍數爾所福聚，能感如來諸相、隨好所不攝、餘大法螺相。由此法螺隨如來欲發大音聲，普能遍告無邊無際諸世界中所化有情。如是無量福德資糧修證圓滿，能感如來不可思議、無上無等、遍一切種最極圓滿所攝自體。
items.en:
Second, examining the store of merit; first, briefly listing what it produces; first, a single pore. In brief, the combined merit of all beings, that much merit gathered together, produces a single pore on the Tathāgata's body.
Second, a single exemplary sign. That same merit, multiplied across all the Tathāgata's pores, produces a single exemplary sign.
Third, a single major mark. The merit sufficient for all exemplary signs, multiplied a hundredfold, produces one of the major marks.
Fourth, the ūrṇā between the brows. The merit sufficient for all the major marks, excluding the ūrṇā and the crown protrusion, multiplied a thousandfold, produces the ūrṇā between the brows.
Fifth, the invisible crown mark. The merit sufficient for the ūrṇā, multiplied a hundred-thousandfold, produces the invisible crown mark atop the head.
Sixth, the great dharma-conch mark. The merit sufficient for the ūrṇā, multiplied a number of koṭis of hundred-thousands, produces the great dharma-conch mark not included among the major marks or exemplary signs — by which, according to the Tathāgata's own will, a great sound is sent forth, universally proclaiming the dharma to beings throughout boundless, limitless worlds.
Second, showing complete perfection overall. Such immeasurable stores of merit, cultivated and perfected, produce the Tathāgata's own inconceivable, unsurpassed, unequaled body, entirely and perfectly complete in every respect.

items.zh: 又此能感諸相、隨好無量善業，當知略由

blocks.text: The marks are linked again to the four ways of practising the perfections (Day 414): resolutely, thoroughly, constantly, faultlessly. Then the treatise tries to express how much merit a single mark takes.

Resolute cultivation brings "feet resting well on the ground". Master Cháng Bǎi: not a needle's gap; one stands firmly. Venerable Miào Jìng on "thoroughly": done finely, not carelessly. On "constantly": saying "it's too cold there, I won't go" is an obstruction.
Not relying on praise, concealing one's virtue, brings the concealed mark. Venerable Miào Jìng: "I don't do good so others will praise me."

The marks and signs exist only as seeds in the body at the ground of lineage; at resolute practice the bodhisattva begins to cultivate the means to obtain them; from pure aspiration on, they are obtained and grow purer (as on Day 439).
They have visible form, easily known by all. Venerable Miào Jìng: the other qualities are mental and not outwardly known.

Merit equal to the total merit of all beings produces a single pore. Venerable Miào Jìng: "all beings" here means humans and gods. Beyond the marks and signs is the mark of the voice, "through which a great sound reaches beings throughout boundless worlds".
"I don't do good so others will praise me." The concealed mark is the reward of concealed virtue: one of the treatise's quieter jokes.

quiz.q: Which mark does resolute cultivation bring?
options: feet resting well on the ground
quiz.why: Resolute cultivation brings feet resting well on the ground. Master Cháng Bǎi: not a needle's gap — one stands firmly.

quiz.q: What does "thorough cultivation" mean, according to the lectures?
options: done finely, not carelessly; all six perfections, in detail
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: done finely, not carelessly. Master Cháng Bǎi: detailed and careful, across all six perfections.

quiz.q: How do the lectures illustrate "resolute" cultivation?
options: Miào Jìng: "it's too cold there, I won't go" is an obstruction; Cháng Bǎi: no circumstance changes the resolve
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: saying "it's too cold there, I won't go" is an obstruction. Master Cháng Bǎi: no circumstance can change the resolve to practise the six perfections.

quiz.q: What does cultivating good without seeking praise, concealing one's virtue, bring?
quiz.why: Not relying on praise, concealing one's virtue, brings the concealed mark. Venerable Miào Jìng: I don't do good so others will praise me.

quiz.q: All exclusive qualities could be called marks of a great being; why are only these thirty-two so named?
options: they have visible form, known to all; the others are mental and unseen
quiz.why: They have visible form, easily known by all. Venerable Miào Jìng: the others are mental and not outwardly known. Master Cháng Bǎi: invisible wisdom is hard to know, so it is not so named.

quiz.q: How much merit produces one pore of the Tathāgata?
options: merit equal to that of all beings
quiz.why: Merit equal to the total merit of all beings produces a single pore. Venerable Miào Jìng says the same.

quiz.q: How far does "all beings" reach here, according to the lectures?
options: both limit it to humans and gods
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "all beings" here means humans and gods. Master Cháng Bǎi: one hair equals the total merit of all humans and gods. The English "all beings" does not note this.

quiz.q: How does the great dharma-conch relate to the marks and signs?
options: outside them both; its great sound reaches beings in boundless worlds
quiz.why: Not included among marks or signs; through it a great sound reaches beings throughout boundless worlds. Master Cháng Bǎi: the Buddha's throat has this form.
